1.pericope_label: Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus; Who was faithful to him that appointed him, as also Moses was faithful in all his house.

schools.summary: Note that both the phrase for holy brethren and the phrase for a heavenly calling occur only here in the New Testament, that the word for partakers is the one used of partners in the fishing, and that the call comes from heaven and is to heaven in its appeal; observe that this is the only place where Jesus is called an Apostle, that the best manuscripts omit the name Christ from the clause, and that there is little difference between Apostle and Prophet so applied except that the one throws the mission into relief and the other the office. Bring in Moffatt's note that the Greek word is the Ionic equivalent of a term meaning not a mere envoy but an ambassador sent with powers, and trace the word for confession through the epistle as a recurring call to fidelity; quote Bengel for the antithesis, that as Apostle he pleads the cause of God with us and as High Priest he pleads our cause with God. Reject the old reading of the verb made as referring to the creation of the human nature, preferring the sentence in Samuel that it is the Lord who made Moses and Aaron.

Gloss the word holy as set apart and adopted rather than spiritually holy, the same sense the word saints carries at the head of the epistles; take the double title as designed for the comparison at hand, since Moses is repeatedly said to have been sent by God, so that both may rightly be called messengers, and observe that the two offices divided between Moses the teacher and Aaron the priest are here joined in one person. Block the christological reading of the verb from the other side: Christ as man was made but not as God, and the apostle is speaking not of the divine nature but of the offices, so that the phrase covers the eternal appointment, the promise, the mission and the declaration at the session on high. Insist finally that the house is God's and not Moses' own.

Take the word holy strictly as consecrated, noting that Israel is called a holy people in numberless places where the people were very unholy, and warn that failing to distinguish actual holiness from the call to it has been the origin of Antinomianism, with its imputed righteousness for unholy believers whose lives are a scandal to the gospel; then compress the two titles into the single word Mediator, since God calls from heaven and to heaven by the gospel. Turn to the verse in Numbers on which the comparison rests, and supply the sense several Jewish writers give the Hebrew word for faithful, one to whom secrets are confided with the utmost confidence of their being conscientiously kept.

Read the word holy as covering both title and reality, so that these are holy not only in profession but in principle and practice, in heart and life; and turn aside to answer those who make the phrase a term of scorn, warning that it is dangerous jesting with such edge-tools, that those so despised should labour to be holy brethren indeed, and that the day is coming when those who make it a reproach would count it their greatest honour to be taken into this sacred brotherhood. Take the heavenly calling as a partaking of the means and the Spirit of grace, a calling which brings heaven down into the souls of men.

debates.question: Does holy brethren describe character or consecration?

sides.position: Consecration only: Israel is called a holy people in numberless places where the people were very unholy, and confusing the two has been the origin of Antinomianism
Set apart and adopted rather than spiritually holy, the same sense the word saints carries at the head of the epistles
Both: holy not only in profession and title but in principle and practice, in heart and life

debates.question: What does it mean that God made him?

sides.position: Not the creation of the human nature, as Ambrose and other Latin fathers and apparently Athanasius held, but constituting, as in the sentence that the Lord made Moses and Aaron
The same sentence in Samuel, with the reference to God
Christ as man was made but not as God; the apostle speaks not of the divine nature but of the offices

debates.question: What do the two titles Apostle and High Priest contribute?

sides.position: As Apostle he pleads the cause of God with us; as High Priest he pleads our cause with God
Both are contained in the one word Mediator, Christ being compared as Apostle with Moses and as Priest with Aaron
The two offices divided between Moses the teacher and Aaron the priest are here joined in one person
The Greek word is the Ionic equivalent of a term meaning not a mere envoy but an ambassador sent with powers

outliers.note: Alone turns the word holy into a warning about Antinomianism, arguing that the failure to distinguish consecration from actual holiness has produced the doctrine of an imputed righteousness for unholy believers.
Alone answers those who use the phrase holy brethren as a term of scorn, warning that it is dangerous jesting with such edge-tools.

themes: holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling
the Apostle and High Priest of our profession
faithful to him that appointed him

3.pericope_label: For this man was counted worthy of more glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who hath builded the house hath more honour than the house. For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God. And Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after; But Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.

schools.summary: Illustrate the comparison from architecture, since the architect is superior to the house just as Sir Christopher Wren is superior to St Paul's Cathedral; but be careful what the sentence claims, since it is not said that Jesus is the builder, only that the relation in which he stands to the builder is set against the relation of Moses to the house, and complain that builded is an unhappy rendering, the sense being one who prepared or formed the house with all its necessary parts. On the difficult fourth verse, admit that the words are clear and the sentiment clear while the connection is not, since if the verse were omitted nothing would be wanting to complete the comparison, and answer either that every dispensation must have a founder or that the clause means simply that he who built this house is he who built all things, God. Call the closing antithesis neat and quite conclusive, since the difference between servant and son is reinforced by the difference between being in the house and being over it, and note that the word for servant appears nowhere else in the New Testament, the Greek translators having felt that bond-servant suited the passage in Numbers less well than attendant or minister.

Prove the superiority by two arguments: Moses so ruled the church that he was still a part and member of it, whereas the builder is superior to the whole building; and Moses while ruling others was ruled himself as a servant, whereas the Son possesses supreme power and had a doctrine committed to no one above him. Note that the metaphor of the house is frequent and well known, the faithful being called living stones and even the vessels with which the house is furnished, so that no one is so eminent as not to be included in the universal body. Confine the words about all things to the subject in hand rather than extending them to the creation of the world, since the point is that nothing is done in the church which ought not to be ascribed to God's power, the instrument derogating nothing from the workman. Read the testimony of things afterwards to be spoken as meaning that Moses, herald of a doctrine published for a time, rendered testimony at the same time to a Gospel not yet to be published.

Identify the house as the church of God, built by Christ who is its head, governor, soul and life, while Moses never put a stone in this spiritual building and was himself put into it by the great Architect; narrow the reference of the words about all things to the two churches, Jewish and Christian, since men may found civil and religious communities but God alone can build his own church, and take the inference as a direct claim to deity. Rest a good deal on a breathing in the sixth verse, observing that the pronoun unaspirated means simply his and aspirated means his own, so that on the first reading the house is God's and on the second Christ's, and that the editions differ; and note that every ordinance under the law was typical, bearing testimony to the things to be spoken after.

debates.question: What is the fourth verse doing in the argument?

sides.position: Its words are clear and its connection is not; if it were omitted nothing would be wanting, so it must mean that every dispensation has a founder and one person stands over both
The reasoning is hard to follow with certainty; the clause condenses the thought that he who built this house is he who built all things, God
The words about all things concern the two churches, Jewish and Christian, not the universe, since men may found communities but God alone builds his own church
They might be extended to the creation of the world but are better confined to the subject, that nothing is done in the church which is not to be ascribed to God's power

debates.question: Whose house is meant in the sixth verse?

sides.position: It turns on a breathing: the pronoun unaspirated means his and aspirated his own, so that on one reading the house is God's and on the other Christ's, and the editions differ
God's house throughout, Christ being faithful as a son set over his Father's house
God's, not Moses' own

outliers.note: Alone illustrates the builder’s superiority from architecture, that the architect stands to the house as Sir Christopher Wren to St Paul’s Cathedral.

Alone rests the sense of the sixth verse on a breathing, observing that the pronoun unaspirated means his and aspirated his own, so that the house is either God’s or Christ’s according to the edition followed.

themes: worthy of more glory than Moses
he that built all things is God
a servant, but Christ as a son

7.pericope_label: Wherefore (as the Holy Ghost saith, To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness: When your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works forty years. Wherefore I was grieved with that generation, and said, They do alway err in their heart; and they have not known my ways. So I sware in my wrath, They shall not enter into my rest.)

schools.summary: Weigh where the opening conjunction lands, whether with the prohibition in the quotation or with the exhortation five verses later, allowing that the writer may have merged his own exhortation into the citation, disposing of the objection that a connective would then be needed, but leaning to the later connection for regularity of structure and because a writer of such manifest tenderness would hardly adopt so stringent a general command as his own. Find in the formula of citation proof that the psalmist wrote by inspiration, and note that the exact phrase occurs nowhere else in the New Testament except once in Acts. Observe that two Hebrew proper names have been rendered by their meanings, that the rebellions they record belonged to the beginning and to the close of the wandering, and that the Greek word for the embittering is found only here and in the Greek Old Testament. Prefer where to when in the ninth verse, and note that in the Psalm the forty years attach to what follows while here they attach to the provocations.

Hold that the discourse is suspended until the twelfth verse, so that the quotation should be read as a parenthesis, while acknowledging that others join the conjunction to the prohibition instead. Explain why the testimony of David is brought forward at all: since the readers were to be sharply goaded, it was better for the sake of avoiding offence to bring another person forward, and a simple reproach for the unbelief of the fathers would have been less favourably heard. Keep two things together on the hardening — that our rebellion flows from no fountain but wilful wickedness, so that the unbelieving are the authors of their own perverseness and can blame no one else, and yet that it is absurd to conclude we have free power to form the heart for God's service, since we have a heart of stone by nature and shall never cease resisting until another is given us from heaven. Take the promised rest as the land of Canaan, so called because nowhere can we have a settled dwelling except where God fixes us.

Warn the hearers that the argument has been put in a manner somewhat difficult and not readily comprehended, and offer to state the whole scope first so that the words may afterwards be clear; explain that the discourse is about hope, and that those who have toiled here will assuredly have some reward and fruit and refreshment. Then distinguish three rests in the passage: the sabbath, in which God rested from his works; Palestine, into which the Jews entering would be at rest from their hardships and labours; and the third, which is rest indeed, the kingdom of heaven, where those who obtain it rest from their labours.

Take the attribution of David's words to the Holy Ghost as proof of inspiration, and use the passage for a longer argument, that these words and others like them imply the real possibility of falling from grace and perishing, without which supposition they would have neither sense nor meaning — asking why God should entreat a man to receive mercy if he has made that impossible, or exhort a believer to persevere if he cannot fall. Set out the itinerary of the provocations from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim and Sinai and beyond; and argue on the ninth verse that the relative should be rendered where rather than when, since when implies the fathers had already seen God's works for forty years at the moment of the provocation, contrary to a history that places the bitter provocation in the third year, citing the older English versions in support.

debates.question: Does Wherefore govern harden not, or take heed five verses later?

sides.position: Probably the prohibition, unless the long quotation is treated as a parenthesis
Hard to decide; but the later connection gives greater regularity of structure, and a writer of such tenderness would hardly adopt so stringent a command as his own
The discourse is suspended until the twelfth verse, so the rest should be read as a parenthesis — though Beza, Doddridge, Macknight and Stuart join it to the prohibition instead

debates.question: Should the ninth verse read when or where your fathers tempted me?

sides.position: Where: when implies they had already seen God's works forty years at the moment of the provocation, contrary to a history that puts it in the third year
Where, literally, as in Deuteronomy
Where, or wherewith, on the best manuscripts; the change is more interesting than important

debates.question: What is the rest they were excluded from?

sides.position: There are three rests in view: the sabbath, Palestine, and the kingdom of heaven which is rest indeed
The land of Canaan, called rest because nowhere can we have a settled dwelling except where God fixes us
Primarily the rest in Canaan and then the heavenly rest in which God dwells

outliers.note: Alone warns his hearers in advance that the argument is put in a manner difficult and not readily comprehended, and offers to state its whole scope before explaining the words; and alone distinguishes three rests in the passage.

Alone uses the quotation for an extended argument that these words imply the real possibility of falling from grace, asking why God should entreat a man to receive mercy if he has made that impossible.

themes: To day if ye will hear his voice
they shall not enter into my rest

12.pericope_label: Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.

schools.summary: Take the second noun as doing the work of an adjective by a Hebraism, so that the sense is an unbelieving heart, and call the combination remarkable, since heart occurs about a thousand times in the Greek Old Testament while an evil heart appears only twice, and since the word here means not so much unbelief as disbelief, a refusal to believe which is no mark of intelligence then or now. Point to the exact contrast the word makes with the epithet faithful applied earlier to Jesus and Moses, and press the epithet living, since the God whose voice they heard is watchful in warning and equally sure in punishment. Turn the warning into a running parallel with the wilderness: these readers too are travelling through a barren waste, exposed to trials, surrounded by proofs of almighty power, seeking a land of rest, and disobedience will exclude them as certainly as it excluded the fathers. Personify sin as the deceiver, luring men away by offering pleasures or by persuading them that forbearance and respite mean there is no living God.

Retain the harsher word rather than softening it, since after men have received the knowledge of Christ their departure from the faith is not mere doubt but perfidy, the wickedness coming first and the unbelief following from it; and distinguish two kinds of unbelief, the rejection of truth first offered and the renouncing of it after profession, of which the second is the more heinous. Describe the descent as a matter of degrees rather than a single act, since we do not fall at the first assault into open striving against God but are accosted artfully by indirect means until we are held in the snare, and only then break out into rebellion. Prescribe the remedy and say why it is needed: we are inclined to evil by nature and want various helps to keep us in the fear of God, since unless faith is now and then raised up it will lie prostrate, unless warmed it will freeze, unless roused it will grow torpid. Locate the particular deceit in the present prospect of relief from persecution, since any sin deceives by some immediate gratification.

Set out the fall as a sequence of five stages — consenting to sin under its solicitation, hardness of heart through giving way to it, unbelief following from that hardness so that the truth of the gospel is itself called in question, evil speaking against the gospel and the provision made for salvation, and finally the falling away, which extinguishes what light remained and leaves a seared conscience and a reprobate mind — and draw the practical inference that whoever gives the least way to sin is in danger of final apostasy. Observe that the injunction to exhort presupposes a settled state of church fellowship, without which they could have no access to one another, and add the counter-example that the fathers had exhorted one another too, saying let us make a captain and return to Egypt.

debates.question: Why is the heart called evil as well as unbelieving?

sides.position: Because the wickedness comes first and the unbelief follows from it; after receiving the knowledge of Christ, departure is not doubt but perfidy
By a Hebraism the noun does the work of an adjective: an unbelieving heart, and the word means disbelief, a refusal to believe
The word stands in direct contrast to the epithet faithful used of Jesus and Moses, and combines unbelief with faithlessness
By five degrees: consent to sin, hardness of heart, unbelief, evil speaking against the gospel, and finally falling away
By degrees rather than at once, since Satan accosts us artfully by indirect means until we are ensnared, and only then do we break out into rebellion
By the trick of sin, apostasy being their peril and always a fraud

outliers.note: Alone sets out apostasy as a sequence of five distinct degrees, from consenting to sin through hardness, unbelief and evil speaking to the final falling away.

Alone works out where the duty of mutual exhortation falls in practice — on intimate friends within the church, on parents over their children, on teachers — observing that a pastor can seldom see the members of his flock in private.

14.pericope_label: For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end; While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.

schools.summary: Fix what kind of union is meant by a figure: the branch to the vine, which is supported and nourished by it, not the ivy and the oak, where the ivy has its own roots and merely clings and climbs; and list what the union involves — feeling, affection, principle, dependence and love, with nothing imparted by us and everything gained. Insist on the tense of the verb, that it is a perfect and means we have become partners rather than simply that we are, and that this is the reason given why they should not be tricked into apostasy. Mark that the word here rendered confidence is not the one used earlier: the first meant boldness, while this is applied to men who make a firm stand when attacked and hold their ground under pressure. Recall that Jonathan Edwards once said the sure proof of election is that a man holds out to the end, and ask what has become of the loud confidence with which these readers began.

Parse the union as three at once — conjugal, so that there is communion of names, persons, goods and honour; federal, so that sin is not imputed and there is no condemnation; and that of head and members, from which come life, grace, fruitfulness and perseverance. Then name the danger the condition is aimed at, that many having only tasted the gospel think of no progress as though they had reached the summit, and so stop not merely in the middle of the race but almost at the starting-posts, and then turn another way; the answer being that Christ has given himself to be enjoyed on this condition, that the same faith which admitted us into a participation should preserve so great a blessing until death, the proof of the reality being perseverance. Take the repeated quotation to show that the reason for making progress never ceases while we live, because God calls us daily and preaching continues through the whole course of life.

Reach the sense of the word rendered confidence from its etymology, that the compound means properly a basis or foundation, something on which another thing is built and by which it is supported, so that their faith in Christ was the foundation on which all their peace, comfort and salvation were raised, and no Christ held fast means no heaven; distinguish what they already possessed from what depended on perseverance, since the present benefits were theirs but the glories of the eternal world only in case they continued; and read the conditional clause as a warning in disguise, since a supposition made by the Holy Ghost is equal to the strongest assertion.

State the privilege plainly, that they are made partakers of the Spirit, the nature, the graces, the righteousness and the life of Christ, and are interested in all he is and in all he has done or will do; then draw the rule of continuance, that the same spirit with which Christians set out in the ways of God they should maintain unto the end, and that perseverance in faith is the best evidence of the sincerity of faith. Warn against trusting to outward privileges or professions, since hearing the word often is a means of salvation and yet, if not hearkened to, exposes a man the more to wrath.

debates.question: What kind of union is being a partaker of Christ?

sides.position: The branch to the vine, supported and nourished by it — not the ivy and the oak, where the ivy has its own roots and merely clings
Three unions at once: conjugal, federal, and that of head and members
A partaking of the Spirit, nature, graces, righteousness and life of Christ, with an interest in all he is and has done
A perfect tense: we have become partners, and therefore should not be tricked into apostasy

debates.question: Where does the repeated quotation in the fifteenth verse belong?

sides.position: With what precedes: either the previous verse is parenthetical, or the confidence is to be held fast in the presence of a warning renewed daily
With the holding fast, though it could be joined to the exhortation two verses earlier if the intervening verse is read as a parenthesis
Most connect it with what precedes, though modern authors treat it as the opening of a new paragraph

outliers.note: Alone brings in Jonathan Edwards’s remark that the sure proof of election is that a man holds out to the end, and turns it on readers whose loud initial confidence has faltered.
Alone parses the participation as three distinct unions at once, conjugal, federal, and that of head and members, with a separate consequence drawn from each.

themes: while it is said, To day

16.pericope_label: For some, when they had heard, did provoke: howbeit not all that came out of Egypt by Moses. But with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness? And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not? So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief.

schools.summary: Decide the accent: the word is interrogative, not indefinite, so that the sentence becomes a question answered by another question, who were they that provoked, and was it not all who came out of Egypt? Note that the oldest manuscripts give no evidence on accentuation and leave the judgment free, that Bengel first recovered the interrogative in modern times though an ancient Syriac version and at least three Greek fathers had it already, that everything down to the eighteenth verse is then a series of questions, and that answering one rhetorical question by another is a favourite device of the diatribe style. Take the word rendered carcases as limbs, from the Greek of Numbers, conveying bodies falling limb from limb; trace the escalation running through these verses, since those with whom God was angry had provoked him, had sinned, had disobeyed and had refused to believe; and find force in the words could not enter, since from unbelief sprang not only disobedience but cowardice and weakness.

Build on the indefinite reading rather than the interrogative, taking some as deliberately softening what David had said more severely, since a few who truly feared God were mingled with the wicked; the milder word both avoids giving offence and sets before the readers other fathers whose faith they may imitate, which would have been impossible had they been commanded wholly to dissent from their fathers. Hold that unbelief was the chief of all their evils and the primary cause of the curse, though it is named last, and trace the sequence forward: having once rejected the possession offered them they pursued their own obstinacy, lusting, then murmuring, then in adultery and heathen superstition, so that every later sin flowed from the same fountain.

Allow that all may be used with propriety when out of many hundreds of thousands only two were found faithful; hear an allusion in the word for carcases to the scattered bleached bones long apparent in the wilderness, standing there as a proof of the crimes and of the judgments of God; pass on the suggestion that the forty years elegantly alludes to the time between the ascension and the writing of this epistle, then concede at once that the dates do not quite agree and fall back on the analogy of crime and punishment; and press the negative of the last verse, that no decree of God prevented them, no necessary strength was wanting and no counsel to instruct them was deficient, since they had all these in abundance and simply chose to sin, unbelief producing disobedience and disobedience producing hardness of heart and blindness of mind.

debates.question: Is the word in the sixteenth verse some or who?

sides.position: Who, interrogative: the oldest manuscripts give no evidence on accentuation, Bengel first recovered the reading, and an ancient Syriac version and three Greek fathers had it already
Who, interrogative, and everything down to the eighteenth verse is then a series of questions
Who, on three grounds: the Greek will bear it, it avoids implying that few rebelled, and it accords with the following verses
Some, and the milder word is deliberate, softening what David had said more severely and setting believing fathers before the readers as examples
Want of faith, the reason distinctly assigned by Moses
Unbelief, the chief of their evils and the primary cause though named last, from which every later sin flowed
Not a decree of God nor want of strength nor deficiency of counsel: unbelief produced disobedience, and disobedience hardness and blindness
Unbelief, from which sprang not only disobedience but cowardice and weakness — hence could not enter

outliers.note: Alone builds his exposition on the indefinite reading that the others reject, treating the word some as a deliberate softening of David’s severity in order to set believing fathers before the readers as examples.
Alone passes on the suggestion that the forty years alludes to the interval between the ascension and the writing of the epistle, and then concedes at once that the dates do not quite agree.

themes: some, when they had heard, did provoke
whose carcases fell in the wilderness
they could not enter in because of unbelief
